robinson_crusoe_day.label: Robinson Crusoe Day
robinson_crusoe_day.intro: A nod to the castaway story that started it all: on 1 February 1709 the marooned sailor Alexander Selkirk was picked up from a lonely Pacific island. A day for adventure books, island daydreams and improvised survival skills.
funFacts: Alexander Selkirk survived more than four years alone on a Pacific island before two English ships took him aboard in 1709.
Chile renamed his island Robinson Crusoe Island in 1966; the neighbouring island is called Alejandro Selkirk.
Daniel Defoe published the 1719 novel without his own name on it, presenting the book as Crusoe's personal memoir.

groundhog_day.label: Groundhog Day
groundhog_day.intro: Every 2 February a sleepy rodent gets to play weather forecaster: if the groundhog sees its shadow, tradition says six more weeks of winter are coming. Equal parts folklore, small-town party and cheerful nonsense.
funFacts: The best-known groundhog is Punxsutawney Phil in Pennsylvania, where the ceremony has been staged since 1887.
Groundhogs are true hibernators: their heartbeat can drop from around 80 beats a minute to only a handful.
The 1993 Bill Murray film turned 'Groundhog Day' into an everyday phrase for a day that keeps repeating itself.

carrot_cake_day.label: National Carrot Cake Day
carrot_cake_day.intro: A cake that smuggles vegetables into dessert and gets away with it. Carrot Cake Day celebrates the moist, spiced classic that tastes best under a thick layer of cream cheese frosting.
funFacts: Medieval cooks sweetened puddings with carrots because sugar was rare and expensive.
Carrot cake became a British favourite during Second World War rationing, when the Ministry of Food promoted carrots as a sweetener.
Carrots were originally purple, white or yellow; the familiar orange varieties were bred much later.

homemade_soup_day.label: National Homemade Soup Day
homemade_soup_day.intro: One pot, whatever is in the fridge, and an hour of gentle simmering. Homemade Soup Day is a hug for cold February days and a reminder that the best recipes rarely need a recipe.
funFacts: Soup is one of humanity's oldest hot meals: cooking pots found in China are roughly 20,000 years old.
The word 'restaurant' comes from French 'restaurer' – 18th-century Paris shops sold restorative broths under that name.
A famous Nebraska study found that chicken soup really does slow certain inflammatory cells in the lab.

chocolate_fondue_day.label: National Chocolate Fondue Day
chocolate_fondue_day.intro: Warm chocolate, long forks and a table full of fruit: fondue turns dessert into a group activity. A very sociable way to spend a February evening.
funFacts: Chocolate fondue is a modern invention: a Swiss chef created it at his New York restaurant in the 1960s.
Its ancestor, cheese fondue, was pushed as a Swiss national dish by the Swiss cheese trade in the 1930s.
Fondue etiquette says whoever drops a piece into the pot owes the table a song or the next round.

chopsticks_day.label: National Chopsticks Day
chopsticks_day.intro: Two simple sticks that have been feeding much of the world for thousands of years. A day to appreciate the most elegant piece of cutlery ever made – and to practise picking up a single grain of rice.
funFacts: Chopsticks appeared in China more than 3,000 years ago and were first used as cooking tools, not table cutlery.
Styles differ by region: Japanese pairs are short and pointed, Chinese ones long and blunt, Korean ones often metal.
Sticking chopsticks upright in a bowl of rice is taboo – it resembles incense burned at funerals.

send_a_card_to_a_friend_day.label: Send a Card to a Friend Day
send_a_card_to_a_friend_day.intro: No occasion, no reason, just a few handwritten lines in an envelope. This day is a gentle push to send someone real post instead of another message that disappears in a chat.
funFacts: The first commercial Christmas card was printed in London in 1843 for Henry Cole; about 1,000 copies were made.
Britain's Penny Post of 1840 made prepaid mail cheap and set off the great Victorian card-writing boom.
Households in the United States still buy billions of greeting cards every year, despite email and messengers.

kite_flying_day.label: National Kite Flying Day
kite_flying_day.intro: Wind, a piece of string and something bright dancing in the sky. Kite Flying Day is an invitation to head outdoors in the middle of winter and look up for a while.
funFacts: Kites were flown in China around 2,500 years ago, long before paper became their standard material.
Before aeroplanes, weather services sent instruments up on kites to measure temperature and humidity.
Alexander Graham Bell built huge tetrahedral kites strong enough to lift a person off the ground.

pizza_day.label: National Pizza Day
pizza_day.intro: Dough, tomato, cheese – and endless opinions about the right topping. Pizza Day celebrates the dish from Naples that conquered practically every country on earth.
funFacts: UNESCO added the art of the Neapolitan 'pizzaiuolo' to its intangible cultural heritage list in 2017.
A true Neapolitan pizza bakes for only 60 to 90 seconds in a wood oven at well over 400 degrees Celsius.
The story that the Margherita was created in 1889 for Queen Margherita of Savoy is a much-loved legend, not proven history.

umbrella_day.label: National Umbrella Day
umbrella_day.intro: A small portable roof that we only notice when we forget it. Umbrella Day honours one of the most underrated everyday objects – ideally on a properly rainy February afternoon.
funFacts: The oldest umbrellas were sunshades; Chinese makers were the first to waterproof them with wax and lacquer.
The word comes from the Latin 'umbra', meaning shade – it was invented against the sun, not the rain.
The compact folding umbrella was patented in Germany in 1928 and sold under the name Knirps.

make_a_friend_day.label: National Make a Friend Day
make_a_friend_day.intro: Say hello to someone new: at work, in the queue, at the climbing gym. Make a Friend Day is a low-key reminder that friendships usually start with one slightly awkward first sentence.
funFacts: Anthropologist Robin Dunbar estimated that people can keep up around 150 stable social relationships.
A 2018 study by Jeffrey Hall suggested it takes roughly 50 hours together to become casual friends, and around 200 for close ones.
Harvard's decades-long Study of Adult Development found good relationships to be the strongest predictor of a happy life.

darwin_day.label: Darwin Day
darwin_day.intro: Charles Darwin was born on 12 February 1809, and his birthday has become a global celebration of curiosity, patient observation and science in general. Finches, tortoises and a very long boat trip included.
funFacts: Darwin's voyage on HMS Beagle lasted almost five years – and he was seasick for much of it.
Before publishing on evolution he spent eight years studying barnacles in minute detail.
His last book, published in 1881, was a bestseller about earthworms and how they shape the soil.

tortellini_day.label: National Tortellini Day
tortellini_day.intro: Tiny rings of filled pasta, folded by hand and traditionally served swimming in clear broth. Tortellini Day is a small tribute to the patience of Emilian kitchens.
funFacts: Legend says the shape was modelled on the navel of Venus, glimpsed through a keyhole by an innkeeper.
The classic recipe for tortellini bolognesi was formally deposited with Bologna's chamber of commerce in 1974.
In Emilia the festive way to eat them is 'in brodo' – in capon broth, never drowned in a heavy sauce.

ferris_wheel_day.label: National Ferris Wheel Day
ferris_wheel_day.intro: Engineer George Ferris was born on 14 February 1859, and his giant wheel still gives fairgrounds their skyline. A day for a slow ride, a good view and a bit of engineering awe.
funFacts: The original wheel at the 1893 Chicago World's Fair was 80 metres tall and carried 36 cars with up to 60 people each.
It was America's answer to the Eiffel Tower, which had stunned visitors at the Paris exposition of 1889.
Today's giant is Ain Dubai at 250 metres – more than three times the height of the first Ferris wheel.

world_hippo_day.label: National Hippo Day
world_hippo_day.intro: Enormous, surprisingly fast and permanently grumpy-looking: National Hippo Day puts the river horse in the spotlight. A good excuse to learn why an animal that can barely swim spends all day in the water.
funFacts: Hippos do not really swim – they walk and push off along the riverbed and can stay under for about five minutes.
Their reddish 'blood sweat' is a natural secretion that works as sunscreen and helps keep wounds clean.
Their closest living relatives are not pigs but whales and dolphins.

almond_day.label: National Almond Day
almond_day.intro: Marzipan, almond milk, biscotti and blossom: the almond is one of the busiest ingredients in the kitchen. February is also when almond trees start flowering, which makes the timing rather elegant.
funFacts: Almonds are not nuts at all – they are the seeds of a stone fruit related to peaches and plums.
California grows roughly four out of five almonds harvested worldwide.
Marzipan is little more than ground almonds and sugar; Lübeck marzipan carries a protected European label.

random_acts_of_kindness_day.label: Random Acts of Kindness Day
random_acts_of_kindness_day.intro: Pay for the next coffee, hold the door, send an unexpected thank-you. This day collects thousands of small kindnesses with no reward expected – and they tend to spread.
funFacts: The phrase 'practice random acts of kindness and senseless acts of beauty' was coined by writer Anne Herbert in 1982.
The Random Acts of Kindness Foundation, based in Denver, has promoted the day since the 1990s.
Naples has done this for a century with 'caffè sospeso': you pay for two coffees and leave one for a stranger.

battery_day.label: National Battery Day
battery_day.intro: Alessandro Volta was born on 18 February 1745, and without his stack of metal discs there would be no torches, phones or remote controls. A day for the humble cell in every drawer.
funFacts: Volta's 'voltaic pile' of 1800 was the first device to deliver a steady electric current – the first true battery.
The unit volt is named after him, and Napoleon made him a count for his work.
The Oxford Electric Bell has been ringing on the same dry pile battery since 1840 and has not run out yet.

tug_of_war_day.label: International Tug of War Day
tug_of_war_day.intro: Two teams, one rope, very little equipment. Tug of War Day celebrates a contest built on strength, balance and teamwork.
funFacts: Tug of war was an official Olympic discipline from 1900 to 1920 before it was dropped from the programme.
Depictions of rope-pulling contests survive from ancient Egypt, China and Greece.
Okinawa's Naha Great Tug-of-War uses a rope so massive it holds a Guinness world record for its weight.

love_your_pet_day.label: National Love Your Pet Day
love_your_pet_day.intro: An extra walk, the good treats, ten minutes of undivided attention: Love Your Pet Day is about spoiling the animal that shares your sofa – and giving shelter animals a thought too.
funFacts: Dogs were domesticated from wolves at least 15,000 years ago, long before farming began.
Every dog's nose print is unique, with a pattern of ridges as individual as a fingerprint.
Cats spend around two thirds of their lives asleep and purr in a low frequency range of roughly 25 to 150 hertz.

sticky_bun_day.label: National Sticky Bun Day
sticky_bun_day.intro: Yeast dough, cinnamon, butter and a caramel bottom that turns into a glossy top once the tin is flipped. Sticky Bun Day is the sweetest and stickiest breakfast of the year.
funFacts: The sticky bun descends from German 'Schnecken', brought to Pennsylvania by German-speaking settlers.
Philadelphia turned them into a local speciality, often studded with pecans and drenched in caramel.
Cinnamon is not a seed or a spice mix but the dried inner bark of trees from Sri Lanka and southern India.

margarita_day.label: National Margarita Day
margarita_day.intro: Tequila, lime and orange liqueur, served in a glass with a salted rim. Margarita Day celebrates the cocktail whose invention story has at least a dozen competing versions.
funFacts: The name means 'daisy' in Spanish; the drink belongs to the classic 'daisy' family of sour cocktails.
The frozen margarita machine was built in Dallas in 1971 from a converted soft-serve ice cream machine.
That first machine is now part of the Smithsonian's collection in Washington.

banana_bread_day.label: National Banana Bread Day
banana_bread_day.intro: The friendliest way to rescue three brown bananas from the fruit bowl. Banana Bread Day honours a cake that forgives almost every baking mistake.
funFacts: Banana bread took off in 1930s America, when cheap baking soda met a general reluctance to waste food.
Botanically bananas are berries, and the plant they grow on is a giant herb rather than a tree.
Nearly all bananas sold for export are clones of a single variety, the Cavendish.

tortilla_chip_day.label: National Tortilla Chip Day
tortilla_chip_day.intro: Crisp, salty, made for dipping: the tortilla chip started life as a way of using up misshapen tortillas and ended up on tables all over the world.
funFacts: Rebecca Webb Carranza is credited with popularising the chip in 1940s Los Angeles from rejected tortillas.
Nachos were invented in 1943 in Piedras Negras by Ignacio 'Nacho' Anaya, who improvised a snack for hungry guests.
Texas made tortilla chips with salsa its official state snack in 1995.

clam_chowder_day.label: National Clam Chowder Day
clam_chowder_day.intro: Creamy, chunky and best eaten by the sea: clam chowder is the soup New England argues about most passionately. Perfect winter comfort food for a cold February day.
funFacts: The word chowder probably comes from the French 'chaudière', the cauldron in which fishermen cooked their catch.
New England chowder is creamy, Manhattan chowder tomato-based – and the rivalry is taken very seriously.
In 1939 a Maine legislator seriously proposed a bill to make putting tomatoes in chowder illegal.

tell_a_fairy_tale_day.label: National Tell a Fairy Tale Day
tell_a_fairy_tale_day.intro: Once upon a time – and everyone goes quiet. This day is about reading stories out loud, retelling the ones you remember badly and inventing new ones on the spot.
funFacts: The Brothers Grimm published their first collection in 1812; later editions grew to more than 200 tales.
Researchers using methods from evolutionary biology traced some tale types back thousands of years.
A Chinese Cinderella story called Ye Xian was written down in the 9th century, centuries before the European versions.

strawberry_day.label: National Strawberry Day
strawberry_day.intro: Red, sweet and the first hint of summer: the end of February belongs to the strawberry. Fresh, as jam or straight from the freezer — as long as somebody is snacking.
funFacts: Botanically the strawberry is not a berry: the roughly 200 'pips' on the outside are the actual fruits.
Strawberries belong to the rose family, which makes them relatives of the apple and the rose.
The garden strawberry was bred around 1750 in Brittany from a Chilean and a North American species.

tooth_fairy_day.label: National Tooth Fairy Day
tooth_fairy_day.intro: A tooth under the pillow in the evening, a coin there in the morning: this day salutes childhood's most reliable exchange rate – and every parent who has ever tiptoed into a bedroom at midnight.
funFacts: Children lose 20 baby teeth in total, so the tooth fairy has plenty of night shifts ahead.
In Spain and Latin America a mouse does the job: Ratoncito Pérez was invented for a young king in 1894.
Annual surveys in the United States track the average payment per tooth – and it has risen well past a dollar.

leap_day.label: Leap Day
leap_day.intro: A calendar day that only shows up every four years. Leap Day is a small bonus of 24 hours – and the reason our months stay lined up with the seasons at all.
funFacts: A year lasts about 365.2422 days, so an extra day every four years keeps the calendar honest.
Century years are skipped unless they divide by 400: 1900 was no leap year, 2000 was one.
People born on 29 February are called leaplings; only about one in 1,461 people has that birthday.
